units.title: Text as bytes: Unicode, encodings and normalization
outcomes: Explain why code-point, UTF-8 byte and token counts differ, including combining marks and control characters.
Defend a normalization and invalid-byte policy, and state which distinctions it cannot preserve.
Predict whether a round trip returns the original text or only its normalized form.
units.why: A tokenizer receives encoded text, not the glyphs on your screen. A silent decoding or normalization change can alter document identity before BPE even starts.

next.note: Use bytes as the complete base vocabulary.
Keep raw identity separate from normalized identity.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 1: Unicode and encodings
study.locator: Sections 2.1 and 2.2, including Problems (unicode1) and (unicode2) (pp. 3 to 5); Section 2.6.2, Decoding text (p. 11)

study.title: Canonical and compatibility normalization
study.locator: unicodedata.normalize: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD, with the cedilla and Roman numeral examples; unicodedata.unidata_version

study.title: Normalization and pre-tokenization
study.locator: Normalization, Pre-tokenization and SentencePiece: normalize_str and the repeated-space examples
study.depth: Stop before Algorithm overview. Use the library calls to inspect behavior, not to replace your later blank-file implementation.

focus: Python len(str) counts code points, not visible grapheme clusters. UTF-8 uses one to four bytes per Unicode scalar value; token counts depend on the tokenizer.
NFC merges canonically equivalent spellings. NFKC also collapses compatibility distinctions; lowercasing and accent stripping are separate choices.
Rejecting malformed UTF-8, replacing it and preserving raw bytes are different contracts. The CS336 text decoder uses replacement, not a reversible arbitrary-byte interface.
Record the encoding, error policy, normalization form and Unicode database version before comparing counts or content hashes.
units.reproduce: Without notes, make a count table for 'é', 'e\u0301', '牛' and chr(0): code points and UTF-8 bytes before and after NFC. Explain why the first two become identical under NFC, but a token count still needs a named tokenizer.
traps: Decoding one byte at a time. A UTF-8 character can span several bytes, so concatenate token bytes before decoding.
Promising raw-text round trips after lowercasing or normalization. Lost distinctions cannot be recovered from token IDs alone.
Using errors='ignore' as cleanup. It deletes malformed bytes and can make distinct raw documents look identical.

selfTest.q: Why can 'é' and 'e\u0301' look identical but have different lengths?
selfTest.a: The first has one code point and two UTF-8 bytes. The second has two code points and three bytes. Both represent the same canonical text; NFC maps both to 'é'.

selfTest.q: What happens to the Roman numeral 'Ⅰ' under NFC and NFKC?
selfTest.a: NFC retains it. NFKC maps it to the Latin capital letter 'I', erasing the compatibility distinction.

selfTest.q: Does complete byte vocabulary coverage make replacement decoding reversible for malformed input?
selfTest.a: No. Token bytes can preserve the input, but replacing malformed UTF-8 with U+FFFD loses information. Keep a separate raw-byte path if that round trip is promised.

selfTest.q: Is chr(0) an empty string or a text terminator in Python?
selfTest.a: Neither. It is the NUL code point, has length one and encodes as byte 0. It may be invisible when printed but remains in the string.

units.title: Byte-level BPE: training, merges and tie-breaking
outcomes: Run BPE training by hand on a small corpus, apply the tie-breaking rule, and predict the merge list.
Implement byte-level BPE training from a blank file, with regex pre-tokenization and special tokens as hard boundaries.
Explain why a byte-level vocabulary encodes any input without an unknown token.
units.why: Every later count in this stage, from sequence lengths to KV-cache bytes, is measured in tokens, and BPE decides what a token is. The merge list is part of the model's identity: change one tie-break and every token ID downstream shifts.

next.note: Turn the merge list into an encoder and decoder you can trust.
Weigh vocabulary size and contrast BPE with Unigram.

study.title: BPE tokenizer from scratch (notebook)
study.locator: Sections 1.1 to 1.4 for bytes, the vocabulary and a worked example, then 3.1 for training, encoding and decoding
study.depth: Skim section 2, the simple implementation. Skip 3.3, loading OpenAI's GPT-2 files, until the identity unit.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 1 handout
study.locator: Section 2.4, BPE Tokenizer Training, with Example (bpe_example) (pp. 5 to 7), then Section 2.5 on removing special tokens before pre-tokenization and optimizing the merge step (pp. 8 to 9)

focus: The base vocabulary is all 256 byte values, so coverage is complete before the first merge. Merges only shorten sequences.
Pairs are counted inside pre-tokens, weighted by how often each pre-token occurs. No pair crosses a pre-token or special-token boundary.
Ties go to the lexicographically greater pair. Without a fixed rule, two correct trainers produce different merge lists.
After a merge, only the counts of pairs that overlap the merged occurrences change. Updating just those makes training fast.
units.reproduce: By hand, train on the CS336 example corpus (low x5, lower x2, widest x3, newest x6) for six merges and get s t, e st, o w, l ow, w est, n e. Then tokenize newest as [ne, west].
traps: Decoding token bytes to str to compare or print them. A merged token can be a partial UTF-8 sequence, so decoding fails or maps distinct tokens to the same replacement character.
Pre-tokenizing before splitting on special tokens. Their text then enters the pair counts as ordinary pieces such as <| and endoftext, and steals merges.
Treating vocab_size as the number of merges. It includes the 256 byte values, the merges and the special tokens.

selfTest.q: Why can byte-level BPE encode any string, while a character vocabulary built from a corpus cannot?
selfTest.a: Its base vocabulary holds all 256 byte values, and every string has a UTF-8 encoding. A character vocabulary covers only the characters seen in training, so an unseen character needs an unknown token.

selfTest.q: The pairs (A, B), (A, C), (B, ZZ) and (BA, A) tie for the highest count. Which one merges under the CS336 rule?
selfTest.a: (BA, A). The rule takes the lexicographically greatest pair, and BA sorts after A and B.

selfTest.q: After (s, t) merges into st, which pair counts can change?
selfTest.a: Only counts next to the merged occurrences. Each neighbouring pair (x, s) or (t, y) loses those occurrences, the new pairs (x, st) and (st, y) gain them, and (s, t) loses every occurrence that merged. All other counts stay the same.

selfTest.q: A training file contains [Doc 1]<|endoftext|>[Doc 2]. What goes wrong if you pre-tokenize it without splitting on the special token first?
selfTest.a: The special token's text is pre-tokenized like ordinary text, so its pieces enter the pair counts and can earn merges. The trainer should split on special tokens so that they act as hard boundaries and contribute nothing to the counts.

units.title: Tokenizer design choices: vocabulary size, Unigram and special tokens
outcomes: Contrast BPE's ordered merges with Unigram's scored segmentations and vocabulary pruning.
Derive bytes-per-token, sequence-count and vocabulary-axis parameter consequences of a vocabulary change.
Define fixed special-token IDs and distinguish trusted boundary insertion from matching untrusted literal text.
Compare tokenizer efficiency on matched language and code slices without treating compression as model quality.
units.why: A shorter token sequence buys context space, but a larger vocabulary costs parameters and output work. Special-token recognition also decides whether ordinary input can impersonate a document boundary.

next.note: Serialize the complete tokenization policy, not just the vocabulary.
Account for the vocabulary axis in model shapes.

study.locator: Section 2.3 (p. 5), Special tokens in Section 2.4 (pp. 6 to 7), and Problem (tokenizer_experiments), parts (a) and (b) in Section 2.7 (p. 12)
study.depth: Use the experiment's matched-sample method on small local slices; do not train the full OpenWebText tokenizer here.

study.title: Reserved-token policy
study.locator: Architecture constraints: reserved tokens cannot be produced from ordinary text unless explicitly escaped or policy-defined

focus: Unigram maximizes a segmentation's product of token probabilities, or minimizes its summed negative logs. BPE follows merge ranks; neither is simply longest-prefix matching.
For B bytes encoded as T tokens, compression is B/T. Compare the same text and preprocessing on each tokenizer, and report per-slice results rather than only a pooled mean.
Adding delta-V tokens adds delta-V times d embedding parameters, plus the same again for an untied output head. Shorter sequences do not make vocabulary costs disappear.
CS336 deliberately recognizes configured special strings. A corpus-facing interface needs a separate policy for untrusted literals and trusted boundary insertion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, score both segmentations of 'ab' with P(a)=0.4, P(b)=0.4 and P(ab)=0.2, and select [ab]. Then derive that 12,000 bytes at 3 versus 4 bytes/token require 4,000 versus 3,000 tokens, or 8 versus 6 length-512 windows if the tail is padded.
traps: Assuming the fewest-token Unigram segmentation always wins. Token probabilities, not token count alone, determine the score.
Calling a tokenizer better because it compresses English prose more. Code, other languages, throughput and downstream behavior can disagree.
Letting a user-typed EOS spelling silently acquire the trusted EOS ID. Decide whether to reject, escape or encode it as ordinary bytes.

selfTest.q: Why can Unigram choose a segmentation that is not the longest available prefix?
selfTest.a: It scores the whole path. A shorter first piece can lead to a larger total probability; Viterbi compares complete paths through the token lattice.

selfTest.q: A 32,000-token vocabulary grows to 48,000 at width 512. How many parameters does one embedding matrix gain?
selfTest.a: 16,000 times 512 = 8,192,000. An untied output matrix gains another 8,192,000; a tied matrix does not.

selfTest.q: A 1,000-byte sample takes 250 tokens with tokenizer A and 400 with B. What is the compression ratio?
selfTest.a: A has 4 bytes/token and B has 2.5. A uses fewer tokens on this sample; that alone says nothing about model quality.

selfTest.q: Does reserving an EOS ID prevent special-token injection?
selfTest.a: No. The encoder must also distinguish trusted insertion from untrusted literal text. Reserving an ID only establishes its meaning.

units.title: A tokenizer you can trust: round trips, identity and streaming
outcomes: Implement encode, decode and reload from a byte vocabulary and ordered merges without changing token IDs.
Test multilingual text, whitespace, controls, overlapping specials and malformed decoded byte sequences against a stated contract.
Preserve one-shot token IDs across streaming splits, retaining unfinished text until a safe boundary is known.
Reject tokenizer artifacts whose vocabulary, merge ranks or preprocessing policy differs from the expected identity.
units.why: A round trip can succeed even when token IDs differ from the model's training IDs. Serialization and streaming must preserve the exact encoding, not just readable text.

next.note: Build training examples from a stable token stream.
Make tokenizer compatibility part of checkpoint loading.

study.title: Encoding, decoding and iterable input
study.locator: Section 2.6, including Example (bpe_encoding), Memory considerations, Section 2.6.2 and Problem (tokenizer) (pp. 10 to 12)

study.title: Saving, loading and reference tokenizer files
study.locator: Sections 3.2, Saving and loading the tokenizer, and 3.3, Loading the original GPT-2 BPE tokenizer from OpenAI
study.depth: Use the save/reload examples as a workflow, not a byte-correctness oracle. Keep the CS336 bytes-based representation and test against tiktoken through the public suite.

study.title: Public tokenizer acceptance cases
study.locator: test_roundtrip_unicode_string, test_overlapping_special_tokens, the two test_encode_special_token_* cases, and test_encode_iterable_tinystories_matches_tiktoken; test_encode_iterable_memory_usage

study.title: Tokenizer identity and adversarial boundaries
study.locator: Correctness requirements: supported round trip and deterministic versioned merges/IDs; Failure-injection requirements: malformed encoding, corrupt model and stale tokenizer

focus: Match exact IDs as well as decoded text. Two vocabularies can reconstruct the same bytes while indexing different embedding rows.
Persist the ID-to-bytes map, ordered merges, special IDs, regex and normalization/error policies. Encode bytes losslessly in the artifact and hash a canonical serialization.
A transport chunk is not a pre-token. Retain unfinished pre-tokens, whitespace lookahead and special-token prefixes; use an incremental UTF-8 decoder if the input arrives as bytes.
CS336's iterable tests use file lines. Add every split point of short strings and splits inside special literals; the public suite alone does not prove arbitrary chunk invariance.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, load your byte vocabulary and merge ranks, encode and decode a string, then serialize and reload. For a short multilingual string containing spaces and a configured special token, assert that every two-chunk split yields the same IDs as one-shot encoding under the same special-token policy.
traps: Encoding every incoming chunk independently. A split inside a pre-token or special literal changes IDs even when concatenated decoded text is unchanged.
Serializing vocabulary bytes as decoded Unicode. Partial UTF-8 token bytes can fail decoding or collide under replacement.
Claiming a fixed memory bound while buffering an arbitrarily long unfinished pre-token. State the maximum-document/pre-token policy and never silently truncate it.

selfTest.q: Why is decode(encode(text)) == text insufficient to establish tokenizer compatibility?
selfTest.a: Different ID assignments or segmentations can decode to the same text. Compatibility also requires identical IDs for the same input and identical preprocessing and special-token policies.

selfTest.q: An input chunk ends with '<|endo'. Can you emit its ordinary-text IDs immediately?
selfTest.a: Not if special recognition is enabled: the next chunk may complete '<|endoftext|>'. Retain the possible special-token prefix until it is resolved.

selfTest.q: A token ends with byte 0xC3 and the next begins with 0xA9. How should the decoder handle them?
selfTest.a: Concatenate their bytes first. Together they encode 'é'; decoding each token separately can raise or insert replacement characters.

selfTest.q: Can a decoder with errors='replace' promise a round trip for arbitrary raw bytes?
selfTest.a: No. It can round-trip supported valid text, but malformed raw bytes are changed. Preserve them with a separate byte decoder if the byte contract requires it.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 1: tokenizer
practice.locator: Problem (tokenizer), Section 2.6; connect your implementation to get_tokenizer in tests/adapters.py and run tests/test_tokenizer.py
practice.note: Implement in your own repository. The encode memory test is expected to fail; the iterable memory test is Linux-only. Add reload identity, arbitrary chunk-split and malformed-byte properties beyond the public cases.

units.stopWhen: The public tokenizer suite has no unexpected failures, and your own reload and every-split-point tests preserve exact IDs while a changed tokenizer identity is rejected.

fit.note: CS336 supplies the implementation contract and checked practice; the notebook supplies reload examples and the project supplies identity and failure cases missing from the line-based tests.

units.title: From documents to training examples: packing and loss masks
outcomes: Derive shifted inputs, targets and valid-loss positions for packed documents, including EOS and padding.
Implement packing with document lineage, a declared truncation/tail policy and separate attention and loss masks.
Keep split ownership fixed before fitting a tokenizer or packing, so evaluation text cannot become training context.
units.why: Packing changes which tokens become context and which predictions enter the loss. An EOS token marks a boundary, but it does not enforce attention isolation or remove an unwanted target.

next.note: Use the valid-target mask in the next-token loss.
Enforce causal and document visibility in attention.

study.title: Shifted targets and sliding windows
study.locator: Section 2.4: EOS between independent sources; Section 2.6, Data sampling with a sliding window: GPTDatasetV1 and stride/context-length examples
study.depth: Stop before Section 2.7. The single-text loader is a baseline; it does not supply document isolation or split-safe corpus construction.

study.title: Data loader intuition with integers
study.locator: Data sampling with a sliding window with number data: GPTDatasetV1, then max_length=4 with stride=1 and stride=4
study.depth: Stop before Finally, a data loader with shuffling. Track indices and the last omitted tail rather than running the full number file.

study.title: Split ownership and packed boundary contract
study.locator: Core requirements: split assignment before leakage-causing transforms and deterministic sample/pack construction with document-boundary/loss-mask policy; Architecture constraints: evaluation data cannot influence vocabulary/filters/mixture; Correctness requirements: fixed split ownership and packed masks
study.depth: Apply these requirements to a few local documents. Do not implement the full project or distributed corpus processing.

focus: Declare whether packed documents may attend to earlier documents. Continuous-stream training and isolated-document training are different objectives; neither policy is created by EOS alone.
For isolated documents, attention allows j <= i only within the same document. The loss mask separately excludes padding targets and cross-document next-token transitions.
Attach EOS to the document it ends. Predicting that EOS is valid; predicting the next document's first token from that EOS is masked under the isolated policy.
Split raw documents or duplicate groups before fitting and packing. Record token spans back to document IDs, and account for every retained, padded or deliberately dropped tail token.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, pack A=[11,12] and B=[21,22] with EOS=9 into z=[11,12,9,21,22,9]. For x=z[:-1] and y=z[1:], derive y=[12,9,21,22,9] and isolated-document loss mask [1,1,0,1,1]. Build the lower-triangular same-document attention mask for x and explain which prediction it does not remove by itself.
traps: Masking EOS as if it were padding. The last content token should usually learn to predict its own document's EOS.
Using only a block-diagonal attention mask. The shifted label after one document's EOS can still be the next document's first token unless loss is masked too.
Splitting after packing or overlapping-window construction. The same document can enter both splits, even when their packed rows differ.

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, which target is excluded and why?
selfTest.a: Target 21 at x position 2 is excluded: its context token is A's EOS, but 21 belongs to B. Predictions of either document's EOS remain valid.

selfTest.q: Does masking a loss position stop that token from being used as context?
selfTest.a: No. Loss masking removes a prediction from the objective. Attention masking controls which input tokens can influence later representations.

selfTest.q: With ten tokens, context length four and stride four, how many complete shifted windows does the notebook loader produce?
selfTest.a: Two, starting at 0 and 4. Each needs five stream tokens to make four input-target pairs; the remaining suffix cannot form another complete window.

selfTest.q: Why split before fitting the tokenizer if no evaluation examples enter model training?
selfTest.a: Fitting on evaluation text still uses held-out distribution information to choose the representation. Fit on training data unless a separate, declared evaluation protocol permits otherwise.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: split-before-fit and split-before-pack, document-span lineage, EOS/tail handling, and independently checked shifted loss and attention masks.
units.stopWhen: Your packer matches the hand-derived inputs, targets and both masks on two documents, padding and an overlength document, with no document ID shared across splits.

fit.note: Raschka supplies shifted-window implementation and index examples; the reduced project contract supplies split and boundary requirements, with packing practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: Provenance, deduplication and contamination
outcomes: Implement stable raw document IDs and retain source, transformation versions and duplicate-cluster lineage.
Remove exact duplicates under a declared byte policy and implement a small shingle-based near-duplicate comparison.
Probe train/evaluation overlap, review false matches and report what the detector cannot establish.
units.why: Distinct files can contain the same document, and distinct documents can share an evaluation answer. Deduplication and contamination checks need traceable identities, not just a smaller output corpus.

next.note: Carry source and cluster identities into sampling and manifests.
Separate observed overlap from memorization and capability claims.

study.title: Exact deduplication, shingles and overlap probes
study.locator: Sections 3.1 and 3.2 with Exact Dedup and MinHash approximate deduplication code; Section 3.3, Decontamination, with word_ngrams and max_overlap; Exercises, Exercise 2: Complete Jaccard similarity
study.depth: Use exact Jaccard as the small-corpus oracle. Treat the four-position MinHash as a noisy demonstration and the stated corpus-removal percentages as unverified examples, not expected results.

study.title: Provenance and duplicate-cluster contract
study.locator: Core requirements: versioned schemas, source/document identities, exact/near dedup and contamination probes; Architecture constraints: raw source identity and separate versioned stages; Correctness requirements: cluster lineage; Failure-injection requirements: hash collision simulation and duplicate clusters spanning sources/splits
study.depth: Implement a tiny exact pipeline and all-pairs shingle comparison. Leave large-scale approximate search and distributed processing for later.

focus: Keep source ID, stable raw record ID, raw-byte hash, normalized-content hash and transform version separately. A normalization collision is not evidence that two raw records were identical.
Use the full digest and verify bytes within a candidate hash bucket. Choose a deterministic representative and retain every removed member's source and raw identity.
Define shingles, Jaccard threshold and empty-set behavior. Similarity is not transitive: connected-component clustering can join two endpoints below the pairwise threshold.

The notebook's contamination score is shared evaluation shingles divided by evaluation shingles, not Jaccard. Common boilerplate can trigger it, while paraphrases and non-Latin text can escape its ASCII-word regex.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, deduplicate a few documents by full SHA-256 plus byte equality, retaining cluster lineage. Compute exact word-shingle Jaccard for a copied, lightly edited and unrelated pair; plant a held-out passage in one training document and emit the matched spans and both record IDs for review.
traps: Replacing a raw ID with a normalized-text hash. Different sources or byte spellings can collapse, and the audit loses their origins.
Hashing and splitting each record independently before handling duplicates. A duplicate cluster can span train and evaluation; fix group ownership or quarantine cross-split matches before packing.
Calling a no-hit report proof of no contamination. Exact and shingle probes miss transformed content, and short common matches need review.

selfTest.q: Two records have the same NFC text but different raw bytes. Which identities should survive?
selfTest.a: Both raw record IDs and raw hashes survive in lineage. They may share a normalized-content hash and cluster only if the declared dedup policy permits it.

selfTest.q: Shingle sets have three members each and share two. What is their Jaccard score?
selfTest.a: 2/(3+3-2) = 0.5. The denominator is the union, not the size of the smaller set.

selfTest.q: A four-word evaluation phrase appears in a long training article. Why can containment be 1 while Jaccard is small?
selfTest.a: Every evaluation shingle is present, so the containment denominator is fully covered. Jaccard also counts the many unrelated training shingles in its union.

selfTest.q: A-B and B-C exceed the near-duplicate threshold. Must A-C exceed it?
selfTest.a: No. Threshold similarity is not transitive. A connected-component policy can group A and C anyway, so document that choice and review its removals.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: raw and transformed document identities, exact and near-duplicate lineage, planted train/evaluation overlap, collision simulation and false-match review.
units.stopWhen: Your small pipeline retains all removed-record lineage, detects a planted overlap and survives a simulated hash collision, with reviewed false matches and explicit limits on any no-hit claim.

fit.note: The notebook supplies executable exact/shingle/overlap examples; the project adds provenance and failure contracts, and the section mini-project supplies the integrated implementation practice.

units.title: Filtering, mixtures and deterministic shards
outcomes: Implement versioned filter decisions and quantify retained documents, bytes and tokens by source and representative slice.
Distinguish document sampling probabilities from token exposure and defend a small source mixture.
Publish deterministic, checksummed local shards and resume without omitted or duplicated records under a fixed configuration.
Use synthetic examples to distinguish PII redaction, toxicity review and quality filtering without claiming production safety.
units.why: Filter and mixture choices determine which text the model repeatedly sees. A reproducible recipe also needs stable shard contents and restart state, not just a random seed.

next.note: Feed batches from a versioned token corpus.
Resume the data stream alongside optimizer and model state.
Extend stable shard ownership to multiple workers later.

study.title: Filter decisions and source mixtures
study.locator: Section 2.1 with quality_check; Section 2.3, PII and Safety Filtering, with redact_or_drop; Sections 4.1 and 4.2 with source effective-token amounts and Recipe A/B; Exercises 1 and 3
study.depth: Skip Section 2.2 and Sections 4.3 onward. The rules and recipe scores are teaching examples, not validated quality thresholds or measured model results. Use only synthetic sensitive-data examples.

study.title: Shard ownership, mixture sampling and iterator state
study.locator: Shard under Split dataset; Interleave, including probabilities and stopping_strategy; Save a dataset checkpoint and resume iteration, including its shuffle-buffer warning; Export
study.depth: Use tiny local records and the six-record checkpoint example. Skip remote corpus downloads, the training loop and Save to the Hub. Library resume is a comparison, not a substitute for testing your own exact-resume contract.

study.title: Auditable recipes and local shard publication
study.locator: Core requirements: mixture weights, deterministic sample/pack construction, checksums, atomic manifests and resume; Architecture constraints: manifests instead of directory discovery; Milestone B: per-stage counts and filter samples; Correctness requirements: complete nonoverlapping shards
study.depth: Keep one process and a few local shards. Leave distributed storage, production classifiers and internet-scale processing for later.

focus: Log keep, redact, reject or review with a reason and policy version. Report yields by source/language/code slice and by documents, bytes and tokens; a smaller corpus is not automatically better.

For source document probability p_s and mean retained length L_s, expected token share is p_s*L_s divided by sum(p_j*L_j), before truncation and exhaustion effects. Declare the sampling unit and replacement policy.
A manifest fixes ordered shard paths, checksums, counts, split, tokenizer identity and recipe version. Publish only complete shards and reject resume under a changed configuration.
Exact resume needs input/shard cursor, sampling RNG, any shuffle buffer and the unfinished pack. HF's documented iterable resume loses buffered shuffle examples; a seed alone does not restore them.
units.reproduce: Build a tiny local recipe that records filter reasons, samples two unequal-length sources and writes ordered shards plus a checksummed manifest. Save the cursor, RNG and partial-pack state, interrupt mid-shard, and compare the resumed record IDs, token exposure and artifact bytes with an uninterrupted run.
traps: Applying English word-length and punctuation rules to code or languages without spaces. Inspect false rejections by slice before choosing thresholds.
Treating email regex redaction or a toxic-word hit as a safety guarantee. Names, context and obfuscation can escape it; benign quotations can be flagged.
Rebuilding shard order from a directory listing or restarting from only a seed. Either can change the next record, duplicate work or lose a partially built pack.

selfTest.q: Sources A and B are sampled equally by document, with mean lengths 100 and 900 tokens. What token share is expected?
selfTest.a: About 10% A and 90% B before exhaustion or truncation. Equal document probabilities do not imply equal token exposure.

selfTest.q: What should you report if a filter retains 80% of documents but only 30% of tokens?
selfTest.a: Both yields and per-slice results. The filter disproportionately removed long documents; neither number establishes a quality improvement.

selfTest.q: Why does HF's iterable state checkpoint not guarantee exact shuffled continuation?
selfTest.a: The documented shuffle buffer is lost on resume and refilled. The saved shard/example position alone does not restore the buffered records or their future order.

selfTest.q: A crash leaves a shard file but no manifest entry. Should the reader consume it?
selfTest.a: No. Read only completed, validated artifacts declared in the manifest. Recovery must verify or rebuild unpublished work before publishing it.

selfTest.q: What does a synthetic toxicity-policy test demonstrate?
selfTest.a: That declared keep/reject/review behavior is implemented on those examples. It does not demonstrate calibrated detection, generalization or production safety.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: reason-coded filters on representative slices, a synthetic PII/toxicity/quality policy table, source token-exposure accounting, deterministic shard manifests and interruption/resume equivalence.
units.stopWhen: An interrupted and uninterrupted small run produce identical ordered IDs and artifact checksums, changed-config resume is rejected, and your audit explains filter yields and observed document versus token shares.
